planting.note: Plant a grafted or air-layered tree in spring after frost danger passes; in zone 9 plant March-May, and like all lychee give it a mild, dry winter chill period to set flower buds reliably.

directions: Wai Chee is a slow-growing, semi-dwarf lychee cultivar that forms a dense, dome-shaped canopy more compact than many other commercial selections, making it a practical choice where space is limited. It ripens later than early-season cultivars, extending the home harvest window when grown alongside earlier-fruiting lychee. The thick-skinned, dull red fruit holds juicy, watery flesh and produces unusually few shriveled seeds compared with other cultivars, improving the amount of edible pulp per fruit. Grow it the same way as other lychee: full sun, acidic well-drained soil, consistent moisture during fruit development, and complete frost protection, since the species cannot tolerate freezing temperatures.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Lychee Fruit Facts
RFCA Archives — Lychee Cultivar Names (Agfact H6.2.7)

planting.note: Plant a grafted or air-layered tree in spring after frost danger passes; in zone 9 plant March-May. Souey Tung is one of the earliest-ripening lychee cultivars and tolerates damper soil better than most lychee.

directions: Souey Tung is a relatively young, early-ripening lychee cultivar that typically matures before many other commercial selections, giving growers an earlier start to the lychee season when planted alongside later cultivars. The tree has an open, spreading habit with sparse, long, drooping branches rather than the dense rounded canopy typical of most lychee, so it benefits from extra lateral space when sited. Fruit is medium to large with thin, dark dull-red skin and a lopsided, slightly heart-shaped form, with a seed that is usually plump rather than shriveled. Unlike most lychee, which dislike poorly drained soil, Souey Tung has a documented tolerance for higher water tables and streamside plantings, though it still needs the same full sun and winter chill period required by other cultivars.
sources: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations — Lychee Cultivars and Genetic Improvement
RFCA Archives — Lychee Cultivar Names (Agfact H6.2.7)

planting.note: Plant a grafted or container-grown tree in spring; in zone 9 plant March-May. Maher is a naturally dwarf, compact carambola suited to containers, so site it in the warmest, most sheltered spot and protect young trees whenever temperatures approach freezing.

directions: Maher is a naturally dwarf carambola selection that stays compact and begins fruiting at a very young age and small size, making it one of the most practical carambola cultivars for containers, patios, and small Gulf Coast gardens where a full-size tree would be impractical. Its round-shouldered, pale yellow-white fruit is low in acid with a mild, sweet flavor, a good option for gardeners who find the tarter Malaysian-type carambola too sharp for fresh eating. Trees are self-fertile and precocious, often setting fruit within the first couple of years from a grafted start, and respond well to light, regular feeding through the warm growing season. Protect the thin bark and foliage from frost, since even brief freezes can kill back top growth on this cold-sensitive species.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Carambola Fruit Facts

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring; in zone 9 plant March-May. Hoku is a University of Hawaii selection with large, elongated, bright yellow fruit, and like other carambola it needs the warmest, most wind-protected microclimate available with full frost protection for young trees.

directions: Hoku is a University of Hawaii-developed carambola selected for its unusually large, elongated fruit with bright yellow skin and matching bright yellow flesh. The flesh is firm, juicy, and notably sweet with few seeds, giving it a richer eating quality than many of the tarter carambola types grown mainly for juicing or processing. Like other carambola, Hoku needs full sun, fertile well-drained soil, and complete frost protection, since the species is damaged below freezing and can be killed outright by a hard freeze. Keep soil evenly moist through fruit development and feed lightly but regularly during the warm growing season to support steady production.
sources: University of Hawaii College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resources — Carambola Cultivars
California Rare Fruit Growers — Carambola Fruit Facts

planting.note: Plant a rooted cutting in spring after all frost danger has passed next to a sturdy post or trellis; Vietnamese Red is a red-skinned, deep-magenta-fleshed dragon fruit sold under this trade name, and like other dragon fruit it needs complete frost protection.

directions: Vietnamese Red is a red-fleshed dragon fruit sold under this name through specialty fruit nurseries, distinct from the common white-fleshed Vietnamese selections more widely grown for export. Fruit is medium to large with greenish-red scaled skin surrounding sweet, deeply pigmented magenta-purple flesh, giving it a more intensely colored interior than the white-fleshed types already common in cultivation. As an epiphytic cactus it needs gritty, fast-draining soil, a sturdy post or trellis for the heavy climbing stems, and infrequent deep watering rather than regular irrigation. The night-blooming flowers benefit from hand pollination to improve fruit set and size, and the plant must be kept completely free of frost, since any freezing exposure damages the succulent stems.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Dragon Fruit Production in Florida
California Rare Fruit Growers — Hylocereus and Selenicereus Varieties
